Traditionalism
truh-DISH-uh-nuh-liz-um
n.
From traditional + -ism; Latin traditio, a handing over, from tradere, to deliver (trans, across + dare, to give). Not to be confused with traducianism, from tradux, a vine-shoot, which concerns the origin of the soul.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Traditionalism is the habit of holding a thing because it has been handed down, and of treating what the fathers did as binding because the fathers did it. Scripture does not despise tradition. Paul tells the church to “hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle” (2 Thessalonians 2:15), and the apostolic deposit is a tradition in the plain sense of the word: a thing delivered. What Scripture condemns is tradition that has come loose from the Word and then been set over it. The Lord’s charge against the Pharisees was not that they kept customs but that they were “making the word of God of none effect through your tradition” (Mark 7:13). Peter says his readers were redeemed “from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers” (1 Peter 1:18). So the line runs between two things that look alike. Tradition rightly held is the church’s memory, a servant that hands on what Scripture teaches: the creeds, the confessions, the hymns, the catechism a father teaches his sons. Traditionalism makes the servant a master. It asks first what the church has always done, and only afterward, if at all, what God has said. The 1689 Confession (1.10) names the supreme judge of every controversy as the Holy Scripture delivered by the Spirit. Councils and ancient writers are examined by that rule. They are never added to it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no entry for traditionalism. Under TRADITIONALLY his example sentence is a Protestant one: a doctrine derived by tradition from the apostles is of no authority. Under TRADITIONARY he names the Jewish party that explained the Scriptures by tradition.

expand to see more

TRADI’TIONALLY, adv. By transmission from father to son, or from age to age; as an opinion or doctrine traditionally derived from the apostles, is of no authority.

TRADI’TIONARY, n. Among the Jews, one who acknowledges the authority of traditions, and explains the Scriptures by them. The word is used in opposition to Cairite, one who denies the authority of traditions.

Key Scripture

Mark 7:8 — "For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men, as the washing of pots and cups: and many other such like things ye do."

Mark 7:13 — "Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye."

Colossians 2:8 — "Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ."

2 Thessalonians 2:15 — "Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle."

1 Peter 1:18 — "Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers;"

Modern Corruption

Traditionalism takes the church’s memory, which exists to serve the Word, and sets it over the Word. Rome made tradition a second source of revelation. The Pharisees made it a fence that broke the law it claimed to guard. A Protestant congregation can do the same thing with nothing more than “we have always done it this way.”

expand to see more

The formal corruption is Rome’s. The Council of Trent, in its fourth session (1546), received the unwritten traditions with the same affection of piety and reverence as the Scriptures, and made the church’s teaching office the judge of what both mean. That is two sources of revelation and one interpreter who answers to neither. The Reformation did not answer it by throwing tradition away. The Reformers quoted Augustine and the councils constantly. They answered it by putting every tradition under the one rule that God Himself breathed out. That is sola Scriptura: Scripture the only infallible rule, and the church’s confessions honored as subordinate standards beneath it.

The Gospel corruption is the Pharisees’. In Mark 7 the Lord takes the case of Corban. The fifth commandment says a man must honor his father and mother. The tradition of the elders let him declare his goods dedicated to God and so owe his parents nothing. The custom began as a fence around the law and ended as a way out of it. That is the shape every traditionalism takes. It starts by guarding the commandment and finishes by excusing a man from it, and the man who keeps the custom feels more righteous than the man who keeps the commandment.

The historian Jaroslav Pelikan put the difference in one line: “Tradition is the living faith of the dead; traditionalism is the dead faith of the living.” Protestants are not immune. A church can confess sola Scriptura on paper and still settle every question by what the last pastor did, defend an order of service harder than the doctrine it was built to carry, and treat a translation, a hymnal, or a building as untouchable. The Lord sends His people back to “the old paths, where is the good way” (Jeremiah 6:16), and the point is the good way, not the age of the path. Age is evidence that a thing may be worth keeping. It is never proof. The cure is not to despise the fathers but to read them with an open Bible, keep what agrees with it, and drop what does not.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Greek paradosis means simply “a handing over.” The same word names the apostolic teaching Paul commands the church to hold and the tradition of the elders Christ condemns. What separates them is where the teaching came from and whether it stands under the Word.

expand to see more

Greek paradosis (G3862) — a handing down; tradition, whether apostolic or of men

Greek paradidōmi (G3860) — to deliver, hand over

Greek patroparadotos (G3970) — handed down from the fathers

Latin traditio — a handing over, from tradere, to deliver

Usage

"Traditionalism asks what the church has always done; faith asks what God has said."

"He mistook traditionalism for faithfulness and defended the custom harder than the commandment."

"Traditionalism, a view of authority, is not traducianism, a view of the soul’s origin."
